title: Review: Tests for ions; Reactivity series and displacement; Neutralisation and salts; Dynamic equilibrium and Kc expressions
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT07#t2 term and clue written for the game; PT07#t4 term and clue written for the game; EQ01#t2 term and clue written for the game; EQ01#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB04#N.10, EQ01#N.12, PT07#N.6, RX09#N.8, AB04#N.15, EQ01#N.3a, PT07#N.14b, RX09#N.6, AB04#N.4, EQ01#N.10a, PT07#N.12, RX09#N.2. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anion
items.clue: The negative particle in a salt, such as SO₄²⁻ or CO₃²⁻.

items.label: Barium chloride
items.clue: Solution added after dilute HCl; gives a white precipitate with sulfate.

items.label: Dynamic equilibrium
items.clue: Forward and backward rates are equal, and not zero, so concentrations stay constant.

items.label: Kc
items.clue: Expression with products on top and each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient.

questions.stem: What are the parent acid and parent base of ammonium methanoate, HCOONH₄?

options.text: Parent acid HCOO⁻; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid NH₃; parent base HCOOH
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₃

questions.explanation: The anion HCOO⁻ comes from methanoic acid; the cation NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ accepted a proton. HCOOH + NH₃ → HCOONH₄.

questions.stem: CO₂(g) + H₂(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂O(g). The forward reaction is endothermic. Which change increases the value of Kc?

options.text: Adding more H₂ at constant temperature
Raising the pressure at constant temperature
Adding a catalyst
Raising the temperature

questions.explanation: Only temperature changes Kc. The forward reaction is endothermic, so Kc increases as the temperature rises.

questions.stem: A student adds barium chloride solution to a solution of an unknown sodium salt, without adding acid first. A white precipitate forms. Why can the student not yet conclude that sulfate ions are present?

options.text: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with every negative ion.
The white solid could be sodium chloride crystallising out of the mixture.
The solid could be barium carbonate, which acid would have prevented.
Barium ions react with water to form a white barium hydroxide precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also white and insoluble. Dilute HCl first removes carbonate as CO₂, so a white precipitate after acidifying must be BaSO₄.

questions.stem: A few drops of bromine water are added to a colourless solution containing both potassium chloride and potassium iodide, in excess. Cyclohexane is then added and the mixture shaken. What colour is the top layer, and why?

options.text: Pale green, because Br₂ oxidises Cl⁻ to Cl₂
Orange, because Br₂ reacts with neither halide and dissolves in the cyclohexane
Colourless, because Br₂ is reduced to colourless bromide ions
Violet, because Br₂ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ but cannot oxidise Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Iodine dissolves in cyclohexane, giving violet. Cl⁻ is untouched.

questions.stem: Baking powder contains sodium hydrogencarbonate and a solid acid. When the cake batter gets wet, the two react. Why does the cake rise?

options.text: HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ from the acid, giving water and carbon dioxide gas.
The acid reacts with sodium, giving hydrogen gas.
A salt and water form, as in every neutralisation, and the steam lifts the cake.
HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺ to the acid, giving CO₃²⁻ and a gas.

questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The bubbles of CO₂ make the batter rise, just as CO₂ from a carbonate antacid makes you burp.

questions.stem: Hydrogen and iodine are heated in a sealed flask at constant temperature until the amount of hydrogen iodide no longer changes: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Which statement must be true of the mixture at this point?

options.text: No HI forms or decomposes now, as both reactions have stopped.
HI forms and decomposes at equal rates, so its amount stays the same.
The concentrations of H₂, I₂ and HI have become equal to each other.
Half of the hydrogen and iodine has been converted into hydrogen iodide.

questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium: in the closed flask both reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of H₂, I₂ and HI stay constant.

questions.stem: A jar of white crystals has lost its label. It could be magnesium sulfate, calcium chloride, barium chloride or sodium sulfate. Which pair of results shows it is barium chloride?

options.text: A yellow-orange flame; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
A brick-red flame; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.
No flame colour and a white precipitate with NaOH(aq); dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
An apple-green flame; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.

questions.explanation: Apple green is Ba²⁺; white AgCl, from acidified silver nitrate, shows Cl⁻. Each ion has its own test.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution: Cl₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Iodide ions are reduced, because they lose electrons.
Chlorine is the oxidising agent, and its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1.
Chlorine is oxidised, because it forms chloride ions.
Potassium ions are oxidised, because the solution turns brown.

questions.explanation: Cl₂ gains electrons from I⁻, so it is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Which reaction produces a salt and water, with no other product?

options.text: Potassium carbonate with hydrochloric acid
Ammonia with sulfuric acid
Barium hydroxide with nitric acid
Zinc with hydrochloric acid

questions.explanation: Each OH⁻ takes one H⁺ to form water: Ba(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.stem: For the reaction X(g) ⇌ Y(g), K = 1.0 × 10¹⁵ at 298 K. Which statement about this reaction at 298 K is correct?

options.text: At equilibrium, the mixture is made up almost entirely of X.
At equilibrium, almost all of X has been converted into Y.
At equilibrium, X and Y are present in similar amounts.
The large value of K shows that equilibrium is reached quickly.

questions.explanation: K ≫ 1, so [Y]/[X] = 1.0 × 10¹⁵: the position lies far to the right and the reaction goes almost to completion.

questions.stem: A white solid gives a brick-red flame. Its solution fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving a gas that turns limewater milky. What is the solid?

options.text: Calcium carbonate
Lithium carbonate
Calcium sulfate
Sodium carbonate

questions.explanation: Brick-red is Ca²⁺; fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky is CO₃²⁻.

questions.stem: Which statement about the relative ease of reduction of the halogens is correct?

options.text: Iodine is reduced more readily than bromine, as it is further down the group.
Bromine is reduced more readily than chlorine, as its nucleus has more protons.
Iodide ions are reduced more readily than iodine, as they are charged.
Chlorine is reduced more readily than bromine, as its atoms are smaller.

questions.explanation: An electron added to a chlorine atom is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it is held more strongly.
